Alexander Pope. An English poet and translator whose career spanned the transition from the Restoration to the Enlightenment. Despite physical disability from a childhood illness—a severe spinal curvature from tuberculosis of the spine that made him four feet six inches tall—he became one of England's greatest poets and the most influential literary figure of the early eighteenth century. His wit, technical mastery of the heroic couplet, and biting satire made him both beloved and feared. His translation of Homer's Iliad, completed between nineteen fifteen and nineteen twenty, was a monumental achievement and a commercial success that became the standard English Homer for over a century. It made Pope's reputation and fortune. The heroic couplet—two rhyming lines of iambic pentameter—was Pope's medium. He perfected the form and demonstrated its capacity for both elevated expression and cutting satire. His original works include The Rape of the Lock, published in seventeen twelve, a mock-heroic poem satirizing the triviality of aristocratic life. A trivial incident—the cutting of a lock of hair—is treated with the gravity of Homeric warfare, revealing the shallow vanity of high society through the poem's elaborate, precise language. An Essay on Criticism, from seventeen eleven, is a didactic poem on the principles of literary judgment that contains several famous aphorisms, including True ease in writing comes from art, not chance. It influenced how generations understood literary taste. The Dunciad, published between seventeen twenty-eight and seventeen forty-three, is a savage mock-epic that mocks bad poets and critics, creating what is one of literature's great satires. Pope's physical reality—his disability made him reclusive—informed both his psychological sensitivity and his acerbic wit.
